summary: Presents what the HPN working group sees as requirements for an IPng protocol set. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A group working on high-speed networks lists what the new Internet design should do.

subtitle: Naval requirements for the new Internet protocol generation.

tldr.problem: The US Navy's mission-critical systems needed capabilities not provided by IPv4, such as multicast support, integrated quality of service, and rapid fault recovery.
tldr.mechanism: The Navy's High Performance Network working group analyzed their application needs across combat systems, general internetworking, and high-speed sensors, then submitted these requirements to guide the IPng selection process.
tldr.outcome: This input highlighted critical needs for mission-critical applications that shaped IPng (IPv6) design, particularly emphasizing multicast as a fundamental feature rather than optional.

facts.label: Platforms to support
facts.value: Hundreds to thousands of large platforms, 500-1000 small aircraft

facts.label: Devices per platform
facts.value: Hundreds to 100,000 per ship or submarine

today: RFC 1679 remains an informational document reflecting late 1994 Navy perspectives on IPng. IPv6, the eventual IPng selection, incorporated many of these requirements including native multicast support, larger address space, and flow specification capabilities that support integrated services.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This document presents the High Performance Network (HPN) working group's input to the IPng selection process. The HPN group was established by the US Navy's Next Generation Computer Resources program to identify the requirements of mission-critical applications aboard Navy platforms such as ships, submarines, and aircraft.

The RFC identifies three categories of concerns: assumptions (functionality that should be accommodated), general requirements (capabilities insufficiently addressed in existing protocols), and additional considerations (important but less certain topics).
sections.plainLanguage: The Navy created a team to figure out what features a new Internet design should have for their ships and submarines to work well.

sections.title: Mission Requirements and Application Areas
sections.content:
The Navy's platforms support three problem domains: distributed combat systems where many information sources must be coordinated into a single operational view; general internetworking for moving information to heterogeneous systems over various subnetworks; and high-speed interconnects for sensors and signal processors.

The applications aboard these platforms require support for diverse information types ranging from voice and audio to video streams and very high-bandwidth unprocessed sensor data, along with services including teleconferencing, video monitoring, voice distribution, and time synchronization.

The Navy systems operate under extreme constraints: platforms must maintain communications while moving, the time frame for deployment extended to the twenty-first century, and mission-critical operations demand high reliability and rapid response to network faults.
sections.plainLanguage: Navy ships and submarines have many computers running different tasks that all need to share information quickly. They need to send voice, video, and sensor data all at the same time without losing anything important.

sections.title: General Requirements for IPng
sections.content:
Addressing: The RFC identifies needs for a large number of globally unique addresses to support tens of thousands of devices per platform and thousands of platforms worldwide. The addressing structure must be flexible and support multicast group addressing, with at least 65,536 globally unique multicast groups distinguishable per platform.

Integrated Services Architecture: IPng must provide mechanisms for multiple service types to operate together while managing traffic flows with predictable delivery windows. Applications in mission-critical environments can have stringent real-time requirements, such as machinery control commands that must arrive before video streams, requiring end-to-end importance assignment.

Mobility: Platforms themselves are mobile, requiring communication continuity as they move between locations. Additionally, systems within platforms may be mobile, such as maintenance terminals moving throughout a ship.

Multicast: The HPN group emphasizes multicast as a critical basic functionality rather than optional. Environmental data needed by multiple systems, video conferencing for operational personnel, and sensor data distribution all depend on efficient multicast. The RFC argues for native multicast support with scope control mechanisms.

Rapid Route Reconfiguration: In high-bandwidth subnetwork environments, the time to detect faults and reconfigure routes must be less than one second, requiring protocols optimized for fast failover.
sections.plainLanguage: IPng needs to give every ship thousands of unique addresses, let many computers listen to important broadcasts, handle real-time commands that can't wait, work when ships move around, and fix broken network paths in less than a second.

sections.title: Assumptions and Context
sections.content:
The HPN group identifies three assumptions about what IPng should accomplish: accommodation of current functionality including connectionless data transfer and support for multiple subnetwork technologies (Ethernet, FDDI, ATM, Fiber Channel, SCI); commercial viability requiring correct functioning, multi-vendor interoperability, and industrial community support; and a transition plan recognizing the large existing IPv4 infrastructure and the need for coexistence during migration.

The group emphasizes that the Navy cannot afford network protocol problems in mission-critical systems and requires a high degree of confidence in both technical soundness and vendor interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: IPng should keep working with old networks, be reliable enough for the Navy to trust it, work with equipment from different companies, and help old and new systems run together during the switchover.

sections.title: Additional Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond core requirements, the RFC identifies concerns that may impact IPng design. Fault tolerance mechanisms including error detection, traffic analysis, and status reporting are desirable. Policy-based routing could support security policies and automatic reconfiguration following subnetwork failures.

Security is essential for Navy applications, requiring support for rule-based access control, authentication, labeling, various forms of confidentiality and integrity, denial-of-service protection, and security management. The RFC notes that the IPSEC working group's efforts should be compatible with IPng.

Time synchronization across platform components is vital, requiring accuracy of at least one microsecond for all hosts in a platform or campus network.
sections.plainLanguage: The Navy also needs ways to detect when something breaks, apply security rules to traffic, and synchronize clocks across the ship so events stay coordinated.

references.text: Bradner, S., and A. Mankin, "IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation", RFC 1550, December 1993.
